entry: Global climate phenomenon that manifests as fluctuations in sea surface temperatures over the tropical [[Pacific Ocean]]. The warming phase is known as *El Niño* and the cooling phase as *La Niña*, with neutral conditions between them. The cycle recurs approximately every two to seven years, with varying intensity, and affects the climate of much of the [[Tropics|tropics]] and [[Subtropics|subtropics]]. The Southern Oscillation, the accompanying atmospheric component, is an oscillation in surface air pressure between the tropical eastern and western Pacific. El Niño and La Niña disrupt normal weather patterns, bringing intense storms to some regions and [[Drought|droughts]] to others. [[Climate change]] exacerbates the droughts and floods associated with the phenomenon. A key mechanism is the Bjerknes feedback, in which atmospheric and sea-temperature changes reinforce each other.

Distribution of electrons of an [[Atom|atom]] or molecule in atomic or molecular orbitals. Each electron is described as moving independently in an orbital, in an average field created by the nuclei and all other electrons. Knowledge of configurations is useful for understanding the structure of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]] and the [[Chemical bond|chemical bonds]] that hold atoms together. An [[Electron shell|electron shell]] is the set of allowed states that share the same [[Principal quantum number|principal quantum number]], n, and can accommodate 2n² electrons. A subshell holds at most 2(2l + 1) electrons, giving two in an s subshell, six in a p subshell and ten in a d subshell. In standard notation, [[Neon|neon]] is written 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Electrons can move from one configuration to another by emitting or absorbing a [[Photon|photon]], and the same idea helps explain the properties of lasers and semiconductors in bulk materials.

Queen of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms (r. 1952–2022). Her reign of 70 years and 214 days was the longest of any British monarch and the longest of any queen regnant in history. She acceded at age 25 after the death of her father, King George VI, in February 1952, and was crowned in 1953. She reigned as a constitutional monarch through significant change, including the [[The Troubles|Troubles]] in Northern Ireland, devolution in the United Kingdom and the [[Decolonisation of Africa|decolonisation of Africa]]. The number of her realms varied as territories gained independence and most realms became republics. She was advised by more than 170 prime ministers and met five popes and fourteen US presidents. Her state visits included China in 1986, Russia in 1994 and the Republic of Ireland in 2011. Her eldest son, [[Charles III]], succeeded her.

American [[Jazz|jazz]] vocalist, songwriter and composer. Known as the First Lady of Song, she was noted for her purity of tone, diction and phrasing, and for her [[Scat singing|scat singing]]. After a tumultuous adolescence she found stability with the Chick Webb Orchestra, and her version of the nursery rhyme "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" brought her and Webb national fame. She led the band after Webb's death and left in 1942 to pursue a solo career. [[Norman Granz]] founded Verve Records to produce her new recordings, which included interpretations of the Great American Songbook. She also recorded with [[Louis Armstrong]], [[Duke Ellington]] and the Ink Spots, producing songs such as "Cheek to Cheek." Her honors included the National Medal of Arts and the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Founding emperor of the [[Song dynasty]] of China (r. 960–976). Born in [[Luoyang]], Zhao Kuangyin rose as a military general under the Later Zhou dynasty, where he excelled in [[Mounted archery|mounted archery]]. His career began at the Battle of Gaoping, against an alliance of the Northern Han and [[Liao dynasty|Liao]]. He came to power in 960 by staging a [[Coup d'état|coup d'état]] that forced Emperor Gong, the last Later Zhou ruler, to abdicate. During his reign he conquered Southern Tang, Later Shu, Southern Han and Jingnan, reunifying most of China proper. To strengthen his control, he reduced the power of military generals and relied on civilian officials. He was succeeded by his younger brother, Zhao Kuangyi (Emperor Taizong).

Study of diseases and disorders in a human population. It is a cornerstone of [[Public health|public health]], shaping policy and evidence-based practice by identifying risk factors and targets for preventive healthcare. Major areas of study include disease causation, transmission, outbreak investigation, disease surveillance and comparisons of treatment effects in [[Clinical trial|clinical trials]]. Epidemiologists rely on biology, statistics, social sciences and engineering for exposure assessment. The distinction between [[Epidemic|epidemic]] and endemic disease was first drawn by [[Hippocrates]]. In 1854 [[John Snow]] mapped [[Cholera|cholera]] cases in London to a contaminated water pump, an investigation that demonstrated waterborne transmission. Later, targeted surveillance and [[Vaccination|vaccination]] campaigns contributed to the global eradication of [[Smallpox]] in the 1970s.

Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer. He led three British expeditions to the [[Antarctic|Antarctic]] and was one of the principal figures of the [[Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration]]. On the Nimrod expedition of 1907–1909 his party set a Farthest South record of 88°23′ S, about 97 geographical miles from the [[South Pole]]. He was knighted on his return. His Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition ended in disaster when the ship *Endurance* was trapped in pack ice and sank in the [[Weddell Sea]] in 1915. The crew reached [[Elephant Island|Elephant Island]] by lifeboat, and Shackleton led five men across the ocean to [[South Georgia]] to secure rescue. He died of a heart attack while his ship was moored at South Georgia and was buried at Grytviken. His reputation was revived later in the 20th century as a model of leadership in extreme circumstances.

Category of sex hormones responsible for the development and regulation of the [[Female reproductive system|female reproductive system]]. The three major endogenous estrogens are estrone (E1), [[Estradiol|estradiol]] (E2) and estriol (E3), with estradiol the most potent and prevalent. Estetrol (E4) is produced only during pregnancy. Estrogens are synthesized in all vertebrates and some insects, and in both sexes their circulating levels are lower than those of [[Androgen|androgens]]. Like other [[Steroid hormone|steroid hormones]], they readily diffuse across the [[Cell membrane|cell membrane]] and bind to estrogen receptors that modulate the expression of many genes. Estrogens are used as medications, including in [[Hormone replacement therapy|menopausal hormone therapy]] and hormonal birth control. Synthetic and natural estrogens found in the environment, called xenoestrogens, are among the endocrine-disrupting compounds that can cause reproductive dysfunction in wildlife and humans.

Method for computing the [[Greatest common divisor|greatest common divisor]] of two integers. Named after the ancient Greek mathematician [[Euclid]], who described it in his *Elements* (c. 300 BC), it is among the oldest algorithms in common use. The method relies on the principle that the greatest common divisor does not change when the larger number is replaced by its difference with the smaller. In the more efficient form, the larger number is replaced by its remainder on division by the smaller, until the remainder is zero. It is used to reduce fractions to simplest form and in cryptographic protocols that secure [[Internet|internet]] communications. Gabriel Lamé proved in 1844 that it never requires more than five times as many steps as there are base-10 digits in the smaller integer, a result that marks the beginning of [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity theory]].

Identity in [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]] relating the complex exponential to sine and cosine. For any real number x, e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x, where e is the base of the [[Natural logarithm|natural logarithm]] and i is the [[Imaginary unit|imaginary unit]]. The formula was published by [[Leonhard Euler]] in his 1748 treatise *Introductio in analysin infinitorum*, and it remains valid when x is complex. When x = π it gives e^(iπ) = −1, a special case known as [[Euler's identity]]. The physicist [[Richard Feynman]] called the equation "our jewel" and "the most remarkable formula in mathematics." It is applied in [[Fourier analysis|Fourier analysis]] and [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineering]], and it represents rotations in the complex plane.

Family group extending beyond the [[Nuclear family|nuclear family]] of parents and children. It includes uncles, aunts, grandparents and [[Cousin|cousins]], who may live nearby or in the same [[Household|household]]. Sociologists find that extended families often remain an important support network even in cultures where adults leave home after marriage. Particularly in working-class communities, relatives gather often for family events and feel responsible for supporting one another emotionally and financially. Sharing a household can help single-parent families meet expenses, though it can burden the few members who carry most of the responsibility. An estimated 49 million Americans, or 16.1 percent of the total population, live in homes with three or more generations. Extended family arrangements remain common in [[South Asia]], where over half of households in [[India]] include extended kin.

French poet and essayist. He developed a form of prose poem that minutely examines everyday objects, as in *Le Parti pris des choses*, often translated as *The Voice of Things*. He was briefly associated with [[Surrealism]], and during the Second World War he joined the [[French Resistance]]. His best-known work, *Le Savon* (1967; translated as *Soap*, 1969), is a long prose poem. He was the third recipient of the Neustadt International Prize for Literature, in 1974.

Conflict between Great Britain and France in North America (1754–1763), generally regarded by historians as part of the global [[Seven Years' War]]. Hostilities opened in May 1754 when Virginia militia led by [[George Washington]] ambushed a French patrol at Jumonville Glen. The British captured [[Quebec]] in 1759 and Montreal the following year, which largely ended the fighting in North America. The 1763 Treaty of Paris ceded France's Canadian possessions and its claim to territory east of the [[Mississippi River]] to Britain. French Louisiana west of the river went to [[Spain]] as compensation, leaving the French presence in North America reduced to the [[Saint Pierre and Miquelon|islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon]]. Over the following nine years, French settlers were expelled from [[Acadia]] and replaced by settlers from New England.

German philosopher and writer. He began his career as a [[Philology|classical philologist]] and was appointed professor at the University of [[Basel]] in 1869. Ill health led him to resign in 1879, after which he lived as an independent writer, moving between [[Switzerland]], Italy and southern France. His philosophy includes a critique of objective truth in favor of perspectivism, a genealogical critique of Christian morality and the will to power. He suffered a collapse in 1889 and spent his remaining years in the care of his mother and then his sister. After his death, his sister Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche edited his manuscripts in ways that critics argue distorted his views, and his work became associated with [[Fascism|fascism]] and [[Nazism|Nazism]]. Twentieth-century scholars including Walter Kaufmann defended his work against that reading, and his ideas influenced [[Existentialism|existentialism]] and [[Postmodernism|postmodernism]].

Austrian film director, screenwriter and producer. One of the best-known figures of German [[Expressionism]], he worked in Germany before moving to Hollywood in 1934 and became a naturalized United States citizen in 1939. His work spans five decades, from Expressionist silent films to his Hollywood career. His silent *Metropolis* (1927) and *M* (1931), a [[Film noir|film noir]] precursor, are among his best-known films. *Woman in the Moon* (1929) showcased a multi-stage rocket and pioneered the rocket launch pad and countdown clock. In Hollywood his films included *Fury* (1936), *Scarlet Street* (1945) and *The Big Heat* (1953). He returned to Germany in the late 1950s, where he directed a third *Dr. Mabuse* film in 1960.

Literary texts written in the German language, including works from Germany, Austria and the German-speaking parts of Switzerland. Medieval German literature includes the Old High German *Hildebrandslied* and the heroic epic *Heliand*, and the Baroque period (1600–1720) was one of its most fertile times. Modern literature in German begins with Enlightenment authors, and [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe|Goethe]]'s best-selling *The Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774) ended the Sensibility movement. Goethe and [[Friedrich Schiller|Schiller]] led Sturm und Drang and Weimar Classicism, and [[Romanticism|German Romanticism]] was the dominant movement of the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Under the Nazi regime some authors went into exile, and others submitted to censorship in what was called internal emigration. German-language authors have received the Nobel Prize in Literature fourteen times as of 2023, including [[Thomas Mann]], [[Hermann Hesse]], [[Günter Grass]] and [[Peter Handke]].

Common, widely distributed type of [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic rock]]. It forms from igneous or sedimentary rocks subjected to high-temperature, high-pressure metamorphism, at pressures of 2 to 15 kbar and temperatures over 300 °C. Gneiss nearly always shows a banded texture of alternating darker and lighter bands, without a distinct cleavage. The darker bands contain more mafic minerals, and the lighter bands contain more [[Feldspar|feldspar]] or [[Quartz|quartz]]. Gneisses are common in the ancient crust of [[Shield (geology)|continental shields]], and some of the oldest rocks on Earth are gneisses, such as the [[Acasta Gneiss]]. Gneisses derived from igneous rocks are termed granite gneiss or diorite gneiss, while those from sedimentary rocks are paragneisses. Its durability and banding make it useful as a building and paving stone.

Web search engine operated by [[Google]]. Launched in 1998, it was mostly developed by co-founders [[Larry Page]] and [[Sergey Brin]]. Results are indexed by PageRank and other proprietary algorithms, and since the 2020s the service has been integrated with generative artificial intelligence through AI Overviews and AI Mode. Google.com is the most-visited website in the world. In 2024 a United States federal court ruled that the company held an illegal monopoly over internet search and search advertising.

Category of plant tissue, neither dermal nor [[Vascular tissue|vascular]]. It is one of three main tissue systems, alongside the protective and vascular systems, and forms the main bulk of the [[Plant|plant]] body. It provides structural support, metabolic activity, storage and [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. It is divided into three types based on the nature of the [[Cell wall|cell walls]]. Parenchyma has thin primary walls, usually remains alive at maturity and forms the filler tissue of soft parts, including the [[Cortex (botany)|cortex]] and [[Pith|pith]]. Collenchyma has thin walls with some secondary thickening and gives extra support in new growth. Sclerenchyma has thick lignified secondary walls and often dies at maturity, providing the main structural support. Aerenchyma, found in [[Aquatic plant|aquatic plants]], is parenchyma with large air cavities that provide buoyancy.

Large 1937 anti-war [[Oil painting|oil painting]] by [[Pablo Picasso]]. Picasso painted it at his [[Paris|Paris]] home in response to the April 26, 1937, bombing of the Basque town of Guernica by aircraft of [[Nazi Germany]] and the fascist government of Italy, during the [[Spanish Civil War]]. Regarded by many art critics as the most moving and powerful anti-war painting in history, it is a grey, black and white canvas about 3.49 by 7.76 meters that depicts grieving women, a gored horse, a wide-eyed bull and flames. It was first shown at the Spanish pavilion of the 1937 Paris International Exposition and toured to raise funds for Spanish war relief. It is exhibited in the Museo Reina Sofía in [[Madrid]].

King of Sweden (r. 1611–1632). He is credited with the rise of Sweden as a great European power, and during his reign Sweden became one of the primary military forces in Europe during the [[Thirty Years' War]]. He is often regarded as one of the greatest military commanders of modern history, using an early form of [[Combined arms|combined arms]]. His most notable victory was the [[Battle of Breitenfeld (1631)|Battle of Breitenfeld]] in 1631, and he was killed at the [[Battle of Lützen (1632)|Battle of Lützen]] the following year. He was assisted by [[Axel Oxenstierna|Axel Oxenstierna]], the Lord High Chancellor, who also acted as regent after his death. He began parish registration of the population, which helped the central government tax and conscript more efficiently. Protestants in Europe commemorate him as the main defender of their cause, and he is called the Lion from the North.

Nineteenth monarch of [[Goguryeo]] (r. from 391). His reign began a golden age in which Goguryeo became a powerful empire and one of the great powers of [[East Asia]]. He defeated Baekje in 396 and captured its capital, Wiryeseong, in present-day [[Seoul]]. When [[Silla]] sought aid against Baekje and its Wa allies in 399, he dispatched 50,000 troops and secured Silla as a de facto protectorate. In western campaigns he defeated the [[Xianbei]] of the Later Yan state and conquered the Liaodong peninsula, regaining the ancient domain of Gojoseon. His conquests reached [[Manchuria]] and [[Inner Mongolia]], and he controlled over two-thirds of the Korean Peninsula. His achievements are recorded on the Gwanggaeto Stele, erected in 414 at the supposed site of his tomb in Ji'an, which is the largest engraved stele in the world. Scholars debate the stele's account of his campaigns.

Arabic term meaning permissible, opposed to [[Haram|haram]] (forbidden). The concept is derived from the [[Quran]] and the [[Sunnah]] and is most often associated with dietary law, particularly meat slaughtered according to Islamic guidelines. It also governs business and finance, including the prohibition of usury, and addresses fairness and the treatment of animals. Jurists have elaborated five decisions: mandatory, recommended, neutral, reprehensible and forbidden, though they disagree on whether halal covers the first two or the first four. In the modern world halal has become a global industry in food, pharmaceuticals and [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]], driven by the growing [[Muslims|Muslim]] population. Concerns about animal welfare have been raised over slaughter without prior stunning, while proponents maintain that the method is humane.

Capital and second-most populous centrally governed city of [[Vietnam]] (pop., 2023: 8,587,141). Located in the northern [[Red River Delta]], it was founded in 1010 by Emperor Lý Thái Tổ of the [[Lý dynasty]] as Thăng Long, capital of the imperial nation [[Đại Việt]]. In 1802 the [[Nguyễn dynasty]] moved the national capital to [[Huế]], and the city was renamed Hanoi in 1831. It served as the capital of [[French Indochina]] from 1902 to 1945. After independence it became the capital of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, and in 1976 it became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Its historic sites include the [[Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long]], Hoàn Kiếm Lake and the Temple of Literature. Its urban architecture combines pre-colonial Vietnamese styles with French colonial buildings, and it houses the National Assembly.

German-born British biochemist. He was a pioneer in the study of [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]] and is best known for discovering the [[Citric acid cycle|citric acid cycle]], often called the Krebs cycle, which allows oxygen-respiring cells to obtain far more ATP than [[Glycolysis|glycolysis]] can supply. The discovery earned him a [[Nobel Prize]] in Physiology or Medicine in 1953. With Kurt Henseleit he discovered the ornithine cycle of urea synthesis, now known as the urea cycle. With Hans Kornberg he also identified the glyoxylate cycle, a variation of the citric acid cycle found in plants, bacteria, protists and fungi. He began his research career in Berlin under [[Otto Heinrich Warburg|Otto Heinrich Warburg]]. From 1954 until his retirement in 1967 he was at the [[University of Oxford|University of Oxford]], and he was knighted in 1958.
